title: You Can Lead Change. You Can't Force Teachers to Own It.
author: David William Sheehan
summary: David William Sheehan uses the psychiatrist Sheehan in Shutter Island to argue that school leaders should enter the world of the people they want to change instead of announcing a mandate and policing compliance. Using a marking-policy example, he shows that what leadership files as resistance is often a teacher protecting a practice that still works, in this case one that takes four minutes a book against the template's eleven. He offers five moves built on the distinction between purpose, which stays fixed, and form, which can bend to the subject and the person, and he says a change is owned only when staff rename it in their own vocabulary. The film's ending supplies the limit: understanding, ownership and adoption are separate events, and an identity cost can lead a capable teacher to decline even a change she understands. He concludes that leaders control the invitation and conditions, not another adult's final decision, and warns against using listening as a technique for removing objections.
points: Compliance pushes after a September rollout often fail by February because leaders treat resistance as a defect instead of asking what the old practice protects.
Separating purpose, which must hold, from form, which can bend, avoids both the rigid rollout and the free-for-all with no spine.
A change is owned when staff rename it in their own vocabulary, and correcting them back to the official term kills the ownership leaders wanted.
Understanding, ownership and adoption are separate events, and adoption can be blocked by an identity cost that has nothing to do with skill.
Leaders control the invitation, conditions and design but not another adult's final decision, so effort should not be burned on the one who will not move.
quotes: What we file as resistance is usually people protecting something that still works.

The department head who ignored the policy was not being insubordinate, she had done a sum the leadership never did, and what the audit logged as non-compliance was a workload alarm going off in the only language available to it.

Keep the first and let the second go. Maths meets the standard with live marking under a visualiser and a coded key; English with fewer, longer written responses; somebody else records voice notes on the bus home.

A change is not owned while it still lives in the leader’s vocabulary. If the head is still saying “our formative feedback framework” and the science team, in the prep room, call it “closing the loop” and have built their own five-minute routine to do it, the change has left the office.
A new approach rarely asks a teacher only to learn something. It asks her to accept that the way she did it for twenty years was, in some measure, wrong.
Understanding, ownership and adoption are three different events. You can see why a thing must change. You can make it yours. You can still decline to do it.

What a leader controls is the invitation, the conditions, the design, the quality of the listening, whether the system can genuinely bend. What a leader does not control is another adult’s final decision.
